newsitem.title: USA: Yeltsin, Russia bask in limelight at G7.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Russia bask in limelight at G7.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin stole the show at the Group of Seven summit on Friday with a performance that shone the spotlight on Russia's economic reforms and kept its financial problems in the shadows.

The seven industrial powers in the G7 allowed Yeltsin to bask in the limelight as a reward for his own role in reforms and for making a deal this year with NATO over its eastward expansion rather than risk a chill in ties with the West.
The 66-year-old president seized the opportunity with an energetic performance which underlined his recovery after months on the sidelines with heart trouble and then pneumonia.
Yeltsin revelled in his early successes at the summit, blowing kisses to cheering admirers and plunging unexpectedly into an adoring crowd to meet local people.
"Denver is good," he said, grinning broadly and giving the thumbs-up sign as he shook hands with people in a crowd of about 200 after talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
The crowd chanted "Yeltsin, Yeltsin" when he suddenly turned and headed in their direction instead of getting into his waiting limousine.
The president, who also blew kisses to a small crowd on the way into his talks with Clinton, looked fit and energetic four months after returning to the Kremlin following his long bout of illness.
Yeltsin told Clinton his main problem was that his suits were baggy because he had lost weight. "My brain is always moving fast, but now my body is also moving with more energy," he said.
Yeltsin had plenty to celebrate. He and Clinton announced agreement in principle for Russia to join the Paris Club of creditor nations, who meet to discuss requests to renegotiate countries' debts.
At talks with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, he pledged to stop targeting Japan with nuclear missiles.

Russia is also enjoying its biggest role so far at a G7 summit, even though it has a much weaker economy than group members -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- and some are wary of granting Moscow early membership.
Yeltsin's warm reception at the summit is largely in recognition of Russia's decision to sign a new partnership deal with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation on May 27.
That agreement helped compensate Russia for NATO's planned expansion into former communist eastern Europe, which Moscow had opposed as a security threat.
Russia's expanded G7 role is a symbolic gesture which allows Yeltsin to present Moscow as a major global power again five years after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
That role, and giving Yeltsin the spotlight in Denver, helps Yeltsin defend himself against criticism by Russian nationalists and communists critical of his foreign policy and economic reforms.
How long the truce with Moscow can hold remains to be seen. France signalled there were still differences, saying objections remained to full G7 membership for Russia.
NATO expansion could also re-emerge as a thorn in relations with the West if the alliance tries to lure in former Soviet republics. Russia has said this is unacceptable.
"Most of what happens in Denver will be intended to soothe Russia's wounded ego," Russian political analyst Viktor Kremenyuk said before Yeltsin left for the United States.
But he added: "Let's not forget that Russia's economy is much weaker than the others'. That makes Russia like a maimed person alongside able-bodied people at the summit talks."
